summary: At two people per square mile, Modoc is the least densely populated county in California — a territory larger than Connecticut and Delaware combined, yet home to fewer than 8,500 residents spread across high-desert plateaus, juniper woodlands, and volcanic tablelands anchored by the Warner Mountains along the eastern edge. The county seat of Alturas sits at roughly 4,400 feet elevation, and that altitude shapes daily life: annual average highs reach only 59°F, nights dip to 38°F on average, and winter delivers real cold, though 8.4 hours of daily sunshine keep the sky wide open and dramatic. A median home value of $212,000 against a median household income of roughly $56,600 yields a price-to-income ratio under 3.8 — remarkably accessible by California standards — and median rent at $818 is similarly low, though jobs are the constraint: the economy revolves around ranching, timber, and public-sector employment (federal land management agencies, the county government, a small regional hospital), leaving very few options if you need to switch employers. Grocery and dining choices are minimal, concentrated in Alturas, and the nearest mid-size city is hours away. Modoc is essentially a place where affordable housing and staggering open landscape come packaged with genuine geographic isolation — the tradeoff is not subtle, and neither is the quiet.
